standard.title: Images, figures, tables, diagrams, maps and graphs
standard.description: identify and explain how images, figures, tables, diagrams, maps and graphs contribute to meaning
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can explain how the sequence of images in print, digital and film texts has an effect on meaning (AC9E5LA07). They have not yet examined how a range of non-narrative visual representations (tables, diagrams, maps, graphs, flowcharts) contribute to meaning in informational and procedural texts.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students can identify and explain how a range of visual representations — images, figures, tables, diagrams, maps and graphs — contribute to meaning in different text types.

nodes.label: Sequential visual representations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify how sequential visual representations (timelines, flowcharts, procedure diagrams, life-cycle diagrams) represent order and process.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain how one type of sequential visual representation (e.g. a flowchart or procedure diagram) represents order or process in a provided text; identify what information it adds that the written text alone does not.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and explain how a range of sequential visual representations (timelines, flowcharts, procedure diagrams, life-cycle diagrams, photo stories) convey sequence and process; compare how different sequential types suit different purposes.
wider: Create a visual sequential representation (flowchart, timeline or diagram) for a curriculum-area process and evaluate whether it adds meaning more efficiently than prose
Compare how comic strips and scientific procedure diagrams both use sequential images — and identify what is the same and what differs in their conventions
success_criteria: Identifies the type of sequential visual representation and names the type of information it conveys
Explains at least one way the visual contributes to meaning differently from the accompanying written text

nodes.label: Conceptual visual representations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how tables, maps, graphs and diagrams represent concepts, information and relationships visually.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain how one type of conceptual visual (table, map, graph, or diagram) contributes to meaning in a provided text; identify at least one relationship or pattern it makes visible.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how tables, maps, graphs and diagrams represent different kinds of information and relationships; explain why a visual representation may communicate certain information more effectively than prose.
wider: Compare the same data presented as a table vs. a graph and explain which is more effective for different purposes
Analyse a map from a curriculum-area text (geography, history) and explain how its design choices (scale, symbols, orientation) affect meaning

response_modes.reason: Students typically have more experience with graphs than with tables, maps or diagrams. Encountering all types across curriculum areas helps students build a generalised understanding of how visual representations work, rather than a graph-specific one.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Cross-curriculum visual literacy work is genuinely rich — understanding how tables, graphs and maps communicate in science, history and geography builds transferable multimodal comprehension skills.
success_criteria: Names the type of conceptual visual representation and identifies the kind of information or relationship it displays
Explains how the visual adds to meaning beyond what the accompanying written text provides

nodes.label: Cultural sensitivity in visual texts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students understand that images and maps may hold cultural significance or sensitivity for First Nations Australians, and can apply appropriate judgement when using or sharing such materials.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify that some images and maps may be sensitive for First Nations Australians and explain why a disclaimer or careful judgement may be required when using them.
nodes.typical_width: Discuss examples of images or maps that may be culturally sensitive for First Nations Australians; explain the concept of cultural appropriateness and how this should shape decisions about using or reproducing visual texts.
wider: Research how First Nations Australian communities manage the use and sharing of culturally significant images and maps, and compare with general copyright practices
Examine the difference between an image that is legally available and one that is culturally appropriate to share, and develop a set of questions to ask before using visual materials

response_modes.reason: Students need explicit reasoning support to navigate the distinction between legal availability and cultural appropriateness — the reasoning chain from 'I can access this image' to 'I should consider whether it is appropriate to use it' requires scaffolding.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations cultural protocols around visual and cartographic materials connect to broader questions of respect, consent and representation — rich cross-curricular learning that extends well beyond visual literacy conventions.
success_criteria: Identifies that visual materials including maps may hold cultural significance for First Nations Australians
Explains why a disclaimer or judgement about cultural appropriateness is relevant when using such materials
